title: Utah drops criminal charges against Kalshi founders after company suspended operations in state
description: Kalshi logo is seen in this illustration taken, August 3, 2026.Dado Ruvic | ReutersUtah on Tuesday dismissed criminal charges against Kalshi and its t
body: Kalshi logo is seen in this illustration taken, August 3, 2026.Dado Ruvic | ReutersUtah on Tuesday dismissed criminal charges against Kalshi and its two co-founders following the decision by the prediction market platform on Monday to suspend operations in the state.The state originally filed the 14 criminal charges against the company and founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara on Oct. 28, claiming that Kalshi operated an illegal gambling operation in the state.The Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator for prediction markets which views itself as the sole body that can develop rules over the growing industry — sued Utah the day before the state announced its charges.Mansour and Lara were slated to appear in a Utah district court on Dec. 4, according to court documents.However, Kalshi suspended operations in Utah on Monday, citing legal uncertainty. Utah Attorney General Derek Brown celebrated the decision in a statement announcing the move to dismiss the state's charges."Every company in this space should take note," he said. "If they promote, support, or enable gambling, we will hold them accountable."Brown's office noted in the statement that dismissal is without prejudice, meaning if Kalshi were to begin operations again in the state the charges could be refiled."Good faith jurisdictional disagreements should never be criminalized," Kalshi's general counsel Yaakov Roth said in a post on X. "We stand ready to work with State AGs on reasonable interim measures until courts resolve the dispute over who regulates prediction markets."While Kalshi faces legal setbacks in Utah, it faced some relief in New York on Monday when a state judge denied an emergency temporary restraining order against the company to halt its operations in the jurisdiction. The court will hear arguments on the matter again in January.Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Utah drops criminal charges against Kalshi founders after company suspended operations in state

title: Drugmaker Insmed shares rally 14% after Sanofi agrees to buy it in pharma’s biggest deal in three years
description: Insmed shares rallied 14% in morning trading Tuesday after Sanofi announced it would buy the smaller drugmaker for $41 billion, marking the largest ph
body: Insmed shares rallied 14% in morning trading Tuesday after Sanofi announced it would buy the smaller drugmaker for $41 billion, marking the largest pharma deal since 2023.The proposed acquisition includes Insmed's portfolio of two commercialized respiratory drugs as well as its pipeline of experimental candidates. Sanofi will pay $175 per share in cash.It's a big bet by new Sanofi CEO Belen Garijo, who took up the role in May to steer the company through its upcoming patent cliff, when its blockbuster immunology drug Dupixent will face generic competition as patents expire. If closed, the transaction will be the biggest one the industry has seen since Pfizer bought Seagen for $43 billion in December 2023.Insmed shares rose 14.3% to roughly $170.40 in morning trading, while Sanofi stock climbed 8% in Paris.'Buys time'Barclays analysts called the deal a "breath of fresh air," significantly improving Sanofi's Dupixent patent expiry outlook by adding Insmed's established respiratory assets Brinsupri and Arikayce, plus a late-stage pipeline offering further potential upside. The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027 and be accretive to earnings by the end of 2028, Sanofi said.Like much of the industry, Sanofi faces a revenue drop toward the end of the decade as top-selling drugs lose exclusivity and open up for generic drugmakers to compete. Global biopharma has experienced a sharp uptick in deals in 2026, as the sector is driven by looming patent cliffs, newly buoyant public markets and a race to beef up pipelines. Following a post-pandemic trough in 2022, M&A activity surged in 2025 and has accelerated into 2026. While companies develop new medicines in-house, acquiring them is often faster and has become the go-to strategy for large biopharma companies with strong cash flows and financial firepower. Investors are also calling for sustainable revenue growth as major drugs lose exclusivity. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconSanofi/Insmed shares over the past 12 months. "Sanofi could offer a far more attractive investment opportunity given the significantly improved growth outlook," Barclays said in a note early Tuesday.Formerly CEO at Merck KGaA, Garijo is facing pressure to find Sanofi's next growth driver. Her predecessor Paul Hudson stepped down earlier this year after the board chose not to renew his mandate, following a six-year reign during which his costly emphasis on R&D failed to deliver speedy results.Read more pharma newsA pharma giant is moving past one patent cliff — but another is already loomingEli Lilly hikes sales outlook, as CEO says there’s room for ‘dramatic’ obesity market expansionNovo’s new strategy hinges on something it can’t manufacture: investor trustCholesterol drug setback casts doubt over multibillion-dollar raceDoctors call Moderna, Merck cancer vaccine data a major advancement — despite Wall Street reactionAstraZeneca may buck a decade of pharma strategy to buy U.S. scaleTrump's generic drug tariffs: What they could mean for medicine prices, manufacturers and supplyNovo Nordisk sues Eli Lilly, alleging misleading GLP-1 advertisingNovo Nordisk's head start on GLP-1 pills forces investors to rethink Eli Lilly's dominancePrices, pipelines and patent cliffs: Inside pharma's big resetUK's biggest drugmakers see surprise profit bump, even as pharma grapples with U.S. policiesThe Insmed deal is a good strategic fit that will help soften the blow from Dupixent's expected 2031–32 loss of exclusivity, said Jefferies analysts. Insmed's medicines Brinsupri and Arikayce could add significant long-term revenue, with forecasts of $6.8 billion and $1.3 billion, respectively, in 2035, the analysts said. They see further potential upside if a settlement delays Dupixent's patent cliff, or if Brinsupri is included in Sanofi's alliance with Regeneron and positioned alongside Dupixent in respiratory diseases."The deal does not fix Sanofi's R&D/pipeline questions, but it buys time," the analysts said, adding that one potential wrinkle is future competition from AstraZeneca's tozorakimab, which is being studied for treatment in bronchiectasis, a chronic lung condition. "Insmed builds on our already successful presence in respiratory diseases through its highly differentiated portfolio, strong science and proven commercial success," CEO Garijo said in a statement. Sanofi shares fell 2.9%, and Insmed rose 24% on Nov. 19 after Bloomberg reported that a deal was underway.

schema.headline: Drugmaker Insmed shares rally 14% after Sanofi agrees to buy it in pharma’s biggest deal in three years

title: Peterson: Here’s what Bessent’s about-face on Jensen Huang reveals about Trump and China
description: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent looks on as he speaks to the media at the World Bank on the day of a meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng,
body: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent looks on as he speaks to the media at the World Bank on the day of a meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, in Washington, D.C., US, Sept. 23, 2026.Nathan Howard | ReutersFor a minute there, it seemed like someone in the Trump administration might actually be willing to stand up to China. For about a week and a half, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was the face of an emerging harder line on Nvidia over the potential risks its co-founder Jensen Huang's affairs posed to national security. Bessent was giving voice to China hawks who had felt sidelined by the Trump administration's willingness to sell artificial intelligence chips to  China. They see China's AI program as a major threat, and want to restrain its growth by cutting off the supply of advanced chips to China. The resignation of Huang, who pressed the Trump Administration to allow the exports, seemed to signal that the hawks had found new influence in Washington. Not anymore.By this weekend, Bessent had softened his public resistance to Huang's reinstatement. That came just in time for Nvidia's board to reappoint Huang as CEO at President Donald Trump's urging.Whether any real damage was done to national security isn't clear. But it is safe to say that the incoming Democratic majority in Congress won't take Trump at his word when he said on CNBC Monday that the Department of Justice "did a pretty good investigation" that exonerated Huang.Congress will look deeply into the worries Bessent himself raised about Huang's acknowledged romantic relationship with a woman The New York Times and others have reported was a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia's board said it had received assurances from top U.S. officials and had concluded his return wasn't a national security risk.A top concern is whether China was able to use the affair to help divert Nvidia's high-end artificial intelligence chips toward helping its military. Bessent in a Nov. 13 interview with CNBC outlined the stakes. "Any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts the — it hurts our great companies and in the AI race it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.Bessent said that his department and others had wanted to blacklist Megaspeed, the company previously run by Alice Huang, Jensen Huang's paramour. But "Commerce has the pen," Bessent said. The Commerce Department is headed by Secretary Howard Lutnick, Bessent's rival.Putting Huang back at Nvidia wasn't originally Bessent's preference. He said in a Fox interview on Nov. 15 that the board should "go outside the company" to find a new leader. But by this past weekend, Bessent had apparently gotten on board with Trump's wishes. "Jensen is on the outside now," Bessent told CBS on Sunday, in trying to explain his apparent policy shift.Commerce has since taken steps to tighten some restrictions meant to prevent U.S. chips from helping China advance in the AI race. But there is bipartisan worry about the Nvidia episode. "I think we need to catalog the damage that's been done," Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., told The Wall Street Journal. He said Lutnick had not responded to letters he sent saying the administration should be "taking the threats of communist China more seriously."But Trump has clearly put an upper limit on how aggressively anyone in his administration can push back on China. The president said Monday that he was swayed by the pageantry in his visit to China last week.Xi "met me at the plane, which is something they've never done, which was a sign," Trump said.Trump said he felt like he needed to intervene to back Huang because the stock market was plummeting in the wake of Nvidia's troubles — a development he also blamed on Democrats' midterm victory. "I watched our country lose $5 trillion because of a bad election," he said. "If I didn't get involved, you'd probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come." Now, its stock performance will be "unbelievable."Bessent on Sunday played down the market risks. The company "continues to be fantastically profitable, and there is near unlimited demand for their chips worldwide," he told CBS.Lutnick has embraced Trump's transactional urges. He has backed deals in which the U.S. takes equity stakes in companies such as Intel, saying the taxpayer deserves some of the upside. Lutnick in January said he had heard Huang pitch Trump on allowing Nvidia to sell its relatively more advanced H200 chips into China."There are strong — two sides. We shouldn't sell them any or we should sell them." Where does he stand? "Right in the middle," Lutnick told Bloomberg. Trump decided to go ahead with the deal.Bessent has said he is "neither a hawk nor a dove" on China, and is simply trying to manage the ultra-sensitive relationship between the world's two biggest economies. But the upshot of the Huang affair seems to be that Bessent wasn't able to sway the president on a matter that seemed cut-and-dried just days ago. Lutnick, meanwhile, is riding high.Trump said he discussed whether Huang should return to Nvidia with Lutnick, Bessent and Vice President JD Vance. "Howard Lutnick was very good. Very, he's very professional," Trump said on CNBC Monday. "I call them the opposites, Scott and Howard," Trump added, before declaring them "both good."

schema.headline: Peterson: Here’s what Bessent’s about-face on Jensen Huang reveals about Trump and China

title: Kalshi daily volume of ‘perps’ trading begins to top its prediction markets
description: This photograph shows set up screens displaying the logo and home page of US based prediction market platform Kalshi, in Saint-Mande, east of Paris, o
body: This photograph shows set up screens displaying the logo and home page of US based prediction market platform Kalshi, in Saint-Mande, east of Paris, on April 29, 2026. Martin Lelievre | AFP | Getty ImagesKalshi is known for its prediction markets across sports, politics and culture. But now, for the first time, perpetual futures, Kalshi's second financial product, has surpassed the notional trading volume of its event contracts on consecutive days.On Thursday, perpetual futures — commonly known as "perps" — on Kalshi saw $3.4 billion in notional volume as artificial intelligence laboratory Anthropic stock debuted on public markets while the rest of the market sold off. That exceeded about $3 billion in notional volume for Kalshi's prediction markets on the same day. Perps are futures-style contracts where there is no expiration and traders do not need to own the underlying asset. Contracts instead continuously track the price of an asset, with funding payments to keep the contract price aligned with that of the market. Funding payments are made periodically between holders of short or long positions. High volume back-to-backPerps trading surpassed event contracts one day in September, but on Friday perps topped prediction markets volume for a second day. Now Kalshi expects that performance to continue as it introduces perps tied to more individual stocks. On Monday, for example, Kalshi launched contracts linked to Anthropic.Kalshi was the first to debut perps in the U.S. after winning federal regulatory approval in May to list perps tied to cryptocurrencies. Perps trading volume includes any leverage that speculators acquire along with their trade, while event contracts are fully collateralized — for now. Since the original launch in May, Kalshi has received approval to introduce perps tied to metals, crude oil, stock indexes and individual stocks. Rapid growth Offshore perps — those available on exchanges not regulated in the U.S. — generated more than $90 trillion in notional trading volume in 2025, so it's not surprising that the product has grown so rapidly on Kalshi, according to Udesh Jha, chief risk officer at Kalshi Klear, the company's clearing house. "We're just in very early innings. We're launching products, we're growing the participant base."Perps were Kalshi's first product to mark its transition from a prediction market-focused platform to a full-blown financial exchange where various assets are traded. Last week, reports said that Kalshi is planning to offer trading on equities on its platform in the coming months. At the same time, the company's perps product has come under fire. Some incumbent exchanges where futures are traded — which saw their stock prices decline following the approval of U.S. perps — believe the product was improperly approved. CME Group is suing the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal derivatives regulator, for approving perps.Efficiency concernOthers have simply expressed concerns about the efficiency of the markets. CNBC previously reported that trading volume on Kalshi's most popular perps markets — tied to bitcoin and ether cryptocurrencies — was dramatically greater than open interest, or cash actively in the markets. It's a phenomenon that isn't common with U.S.-regulated traditional futures, nor other offshore perps markets. Kalshi said at the time it has "zero concerns" about the distinction, and that it appears because less leverage is offered compared to offshore exchanges and there are fewer incentives for traders to park capital on its perps markets. While Kalshi started with cryptocurrencies, Owen Lau, an analyst at Clear Street, said perps tied to individual stocks likely represent the most promising opportunity for growth in the U.S. "That's how I foresee the way perps will penetrate further into traditional asset classes," Lau said. "Perps on single stocks and [key performance indicators on individual companies] could change how investors hedge their portfolio or even make a directional bet."Monopoly statusKalshi's growth has been powered by the fact that right now it's the only exchange that can actively list perps in the U.S., though crypto exchange Coinbase received approval in May to route U.S. users to offshore platforms for trading. That monopoly status, however, will probably prove short lived. Coinbase has filed to list single-stock perps in the U.S., and President Donald Trump in August said the CFTC is working to bring Hyperliquid — a dominant player in offshore perps activity — to domestic traders. But Jha at Kalshi isn't worried about the competition."What will carry us is ... making sure that we have the right products for the marketplace, making sure we have the right surveillance of the products that we are trading."Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Kalshi daily volume of ‘perps’ trading begins to top its prediction markets

title: Fed's John Williams indicates higher interest rates likely 'over time' to address inflation
description: John Williams, president and chief executive officer of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, speaks during an Economic Club of New York (ECNY) event
body: John Williams, president and chief executive officer of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, speaks during an Economic Club of New York (ECNY) event in New York, US, on Thursday, Sept. 4, 2025.David Dee Delgado | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesNew York Federal Reserve President John Williams said Monday that policymakers have more work to do to bring inflation under control, though he indicated that further action can unfold over time as the economy continues to grow.In remarks consistent with previous statements, the influential central banker expressed confidence that inflation will get closer to the Fed's 2% target in 2027 before hitting the goal the following year. He also said that while artificial intelligence is pressuring prices, there's "little evidence" it will be the source of more persistent inflation."But getting inflation back to 2% is 100% essential," he said in remarks at the University of Mount Saint Vincent in New York. "We must take actions over time that will ensure that we get inflation back to our 2% goal in a timely manner and on a sustained basis. There is still work to do to get that done."The comments come at a delicate moment for monetary policy, as the economy continues to grow and inflation stays well above the Fed's goal. Fed officials have differed over how quickly to raise rates, with some advocating more aggressive action while others, including Williams, have emphasized a measured approach.Williams ascribed the current inflation pressures to the conflict in Iran, demand for goods associated with the AI build-out and tariffs, the effects of which he said "have largely abated" as a source of pressure. Nevertheless, he expressed confidence that inflation will subside substantially in 2027 even as economic growth remains robust and unemployment edges lower.The Federal Open Market Committee next meets on Dec. 8-9, with markets fully pricing in a quarter percentage point interest rate increase from the current target range of 3.75%-4%. The remarks from Williams are expected to be the last major policy statement from any Fed official before the December decision."Monetary policy cannot move ships or reopen pipelines and refineries, but it can — and must — ensure that these shocks do not lead to broader or persistent inflationary dynamics or erode well-anchored inflation expectations," Williams said, according to his prepared remarks.Williams did not explicitly address the December meeting expectations, instead pointing to the statement released after the prior FOMC meeting in late October that said the "accumulation of more information" will help decide the future policy path. "The data that we have received since then show that the economy has remained strong and that inflation has continued to run too high," he said.

schema.headline: Fed's John Williams indicates higher interest rates likely 'over time' to address inflation

title: Retail turnarounds are taking hold just in time for the holiday season
description: A customer shops at a Target store, Nov. 18, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. Scott Olson | Getty ImagesOnce-struggling retailers are entering the holiday q
body: A customer shops at a Target store, Nov. 18, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. Scott Olson | Getty ImagesOnce-struggling retailers are entering the holiday quarter with improved performance and sales momentum as turnaround efforts begin to resonate with shoppers. A handful of earnings reports on Tuesday pointed to a mix of factors behind the strong results, including a resilient consumer, stronger execution and demand for the right products at the right price.Kohl's reported comparable sales growth of 1.2% for the period ended Oct. 31 and raised its full-year outlook as CEO Michael Bender said customers "have remained resilient" but are "migrating to value with their purchases." He tied improvement to the company's work on product assortment, store experience and value.Best Buy also on Tuesday posted its highest comparable sales growth in five years, at 6.1%, which prompted the electronics retailer to raise its full-year outlook. "We have a tremendous amount of momentum," CEO Jason Bonfig told CNBC in an interview. "The fact that we saw pretty much broad-based growth across almost all of our categories is a lot of momentum that we're very excited about."Signage for a Best Buy store location in Brampton, Ontario, on May 27, 2026. Mike Campbell | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesThe company also credited execution, market share gains and a compelling product cycle alongside growing customer demand. At Dick's Sporting Goods, quarterly comparable sales rose 2.6% at the core business and 0.5% at Foot Locker. CEO Lauren Hobart said "all income demographics grew" and the company "didn't see trade-down from best to better or better to good." She similarly pointed to new products and market share gains within the category as contributing to the strong quarter. She also highlighted continued improvement at Foot Locker.All three companies have been undergoing efforts to boost sales and get the right products on shelves to meet customer demand. Target, likewise undergoing revitalization efforts, last week reported comparable sales growth of 5.6% in the third quarter, fueled by a 5% increase in comparable traffic. The retailer raised its full-year outlook. CEO Michael Fiddelke at the time called the traffic gain "a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often."Even Gap CEO Richard Dickson told CNBC the company has moved from "rebuild mode" to "turnaround mode" at its Old Navy banner, a sign of progress, albeit not a broad-based portfolio recovery.Michael Baker, a retail analyst at D.A. Davidson, told CNBC he sees both a resilient consumer and company-specific improvements as driving sector strength. "Retail sales have been more resilient than most think," Baker said. His analysis showed retail sales, excluding autos and gas, rose 5.1% in the third quarter on a non-seasonally adjusted basis — the strongest quarter since the pandemic.But he cautioned that growth appears to be coming more from transaction size than traffic, with inflation, promotions and higher units per transaction driving up spend. A Dollar Tree store in Denver, Colorado, US, on Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. Chet Strange | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesDollar Tree, which reported better-than-expected earnings on Tuesday morning, posted a 3.8% increase to traffic, accelerating from 0.4% growth in the prior quarter, suggesting more shoppers may be bargain hunting. Comparable sales at the retailer increased 4.6% during the period. "Consumers are under pressure, and they are increasingly selective about where and how they spend," said Dollar Tree CEO Michael Creedon on the company's earnings call. "When under pressure, shoppers prioritize value and buy closer to need." Comparable sales of everyday essentials rose 8.9% at Dollar Tree stores in the third quarter, while sales of nonessential items were essentially flat, the company said. — CNBC's Laya Neelakandan contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Retail turnarounds are taking hold just in time for the holiday season

title: Consumer confidence shoots up after Democrats' midterm victories — though inflation worries persist
description: A couple looks at a frozen food display while shopping at a Costco Wholesale store on Sept. 25, 2026 in Colchester, Vermont. Robert Nickelsberg | Gett
body: A couple looks at a frozen food display while shopping at a Costco Wholesale store on Sept. 25, 2026 in Colchester, Vermont. Robert Nickelsberg | Getty ImagesConsumers grew significantly more optimistic in November in the wake of the midterm elections, with a growing number of Americans now seeing improvement in the labor market and expecting inflation to cool. The Conference Board survey released Tuesday showed improvement across the board, with the headline confidence index jumping to 103.3, up 11.4 points from October and much better than the Dow Jones consensus forecast for 92.2.Confidence among Democrats and independent voters improved sharply, the Conference Board said, while confidence among Republican respondents fell slightly. Still, confidence among Republicans remained the highest among the three groups.While respondents "continued to express frustration with high prices and rising costs," they also "cited hope for the general economy," said Fergus McCormick, the board's senior economist for global indicators.The survey comes with the Federal Reserve continuing to try to bring down inflation, which has run above the central bank's 2% target for some 5½ years. The Fed is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point when it meets again in two weeks.Despite the lingering worries about the cost of living — a centerpiece issue during the midterms — the survey's present situation and expectations indexes both posted strong gains. Inflation expectations for 12 months from now fell for the second straight month but remained high at 5.7%.The survey's closely watched gap between jobs considered "plentiful" versus "hard to get" widened to 12.4 percentage points. The "plentiful" side rose to 30.8% from 26.2% while "hard to get" fell to 18.4%, down 3 percentage points.The survey results are the second in the past week to reveal that Americans are growing more optimistic about the economy. The University of Michigan's November survey, released Friday, showed a 7.3% increase since October, with a similar partisan split.

schema.headline: Consumer confidence shoots up after Democrats' midterm victories — though inflation worries persist

title: Some U.S. food banks see demand top pandemic levels
description: watch nowDuring the Covid-19 pandemic, Greg Silverman watched an MTA bus driver pull over on Manhattan's Upper West Side, let his passengers off and r
body: watch nowDuring the Covid-19 pandemic, Greg Silverman watched an MTA bus driver pull over on Manhattan's Upper West Side, let his passengers off and run across the street toward him.Silverman, who runs New York nonprofit West Side Campaign Against Hunger, initially thought the driver wanted to use the bathroom at the church where the food distribution was taking place. Instead, the man asked, "Can I get some food?""He was a full-time employee," Silverman said. "You are an essential personnel, making the city survive and you need food."Now, Silverman said, his organization has seen demand surpass even the levels it observed during that time of crisis when the U.S. economy ground to a halt — and many of the people now seeking food also have jobs. Silverman expects the nonprofit to distribute as much as 6 million pounds of food this year."The height of the pandemic was not the height of need, by any means," he said. Echoes of the pandemicVolunteers Valentin Flores, left, and Keith Harrison load boxes of food for Thanksgiving at the parking lot of Dick's Sporting Goods Park in Commerce City, Colorado, Nov. 20, 2026.Hyoung Chang | Denver Post | Getty ImagesThe pressure on the emergency food system extends beyond New York. Nationally, use of charitable food programs remains elevated as sustained inflation makes it harder for Americans to afford food, housing and healthcare. Higher prices come at the same time that the federal government has restricted food aid. The Department of Agriculture's latest annual report found that 13.7% of U.S. households, roughly 18.3 million households, experienced food insecurity in 2024. That rate was significantly higher than in every year from 2016 through 2021.The pandemic initially brought a surge in demand for charitable food programs, which was followed by government support. In the years that followed, pandemic-era policies such as expanded Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, benefits, the enhanced child tax credit and school meal programs phased out as inflation spiked."This is not because you can't go to work," said City Harvest President Carlos Rodriguez. "Primarily, your work and your wages are just not keeping up with the way costs have gone up in the last five years alone."City Harvest, which works with food providers across the five boroughs of New York, told CNBC 1 in 5 New Yorkers is currently experiencing food insecurity, or limited access to enough food because of a lack of money or other resources. That is up from 1 in 6 a year earlier, and 1 in 8 before the pandemic. Average monthly visits to food pantries and soup kitchens in New York are also 85% higher than before the pandemic, said Rodriguez.In the Federal Reserve's October Beige Book, the central bank's New York regional branch described a sharp rise in first-time food pantry users. One nonprofit leader told the Federal Reserve Bank of New York that the strain was comparable to the pandemic, "but without the same philanthropic and government support."Data from Plentiful, a technology platform that connects people with food pantries and tracks their usage, also points to growing demand and limited resources."For pantries using our reservation and pre-registration features, we see that the overwhelming majority of those are at or over capacity," said Catherine Compitello, CEO of Plentiful. "Demand is growing while supply is not."First-time users of Plentiful in New York City rose roughly 56% from August to October, Compitello said. It was the second-largest fall surge since 2016; the only larger one came during last year's federal government shutdown, when delayed SNAP benefits drove more people to seek food assistance.Compitello said that when families have trouble affording essentials, they often prioritize healthcare, transportation, childcare and utilities, leaving food as the expense they cut back on.Hunger around the countryStaff distribute food at the Bounty & Soul food bank in Asheville, North Carolina, Oct. 30, 2026.Allison Joyce | Getty ImagesDemand for food banks is rising in other regions of the country, and nonprofits are facing their own operational challenges as they try to meet it.A spokesperson for the Los Angeles Regional Food Bank told CNBC the organization's diesel bill more than doubled in September, to roughly $75,000, adding to the cost of delivering food and running refrigerated trucks.Demand in the region is also spiking. Distribution in the Los Angeles area for January through September totaled 116 million pounds of food and grocery products — the equivalent of 93 million meals — and slightly higher than a near-record year in 2025, according to the Los Angeles Regional Food Bank.Federal food aid changes have exacerbated the problems. Rodriguez of City Harvest described SNAP as a first line of defense against hunger, saying the program can provide as many as nine meals for every one meal the organization provides. But City Harvest has estimated at least 8.7% of SNAP recipients in New York City lost benefits over the past year, after congressional Republicans and President Donald Trump approved work certification requirements and changes to eligibility.The pressure is also mounting in Los Angeles County, where roughly 260,000 CalFresh recipients are subject to expanded federal work requirements that took effect in June. CalFresh is California's version of SNAP. That does not mean all 260,000 will lose benefits, since people who meet the work requirements or qualify for an exemption can remain eligible. But a Los Angeles Regional Food Bank spokesperson told CNBC the changes add another layer of uncertainty for households already struggling with food costs.In Atlanta, the pressure extends beyond the city itself to the surrounding region. The Atlanta Community Food Bank serves about 270,000 households a month, or nearly 700,000 people, through partner pantries across North Georgia. President and CEO Kyle Waide said the number of people it serves has jumped more than 70% in five years."Much of that increase is among people whose incomes are too high to qualify for federal benefit programs," said Waide.Under current SNAP guidelines in Georgia, most households must have gross monthly income at or below 130% of the federal poverty level to qualify. They must also meet a separate net income test. For fiscal 2027, which began Oct. 1, the gross income limit is $2,960 a month for a household of three, or about $35,520 annually, and $3,575 a month for a household of four, or $42,900 a year.More than 60% of Atlanta Community Food Bank clients have household incomes above the cutoff for SNAP eligibility, Waide said, generally in the mid-to-upper $30,000 range depending on household size. The food bank does not collect everyone's income, he said, but the figure is based on survey estimates.Given those dynamics, Waide said he does not expect the need to ease. "We're preparing for the level of demand to stay where it is today, or even increase more," Waide said. "We don't see a big source of relief coming anytime soon."

schema.headline: Some U.S. food banks see demand top pandemic levels

title: AG Blanche, FBI’s Patel dodge questions about Jensen Huang investigation
description: FBI Director Kash Patel speaks alongside US Attorney General Todd Blanche (L) during a news conference to announce the results of a crackdown on cyber
body: FBI Director Kash Patel speaks alongside US Attorney General Todd Blanche (L) during a news conference to announce the results of a crackdown on cyber-enabled scams, at the Department of Justice in Washington, DC, Nov. 24, 2026. Ken Cedeno | AFP | Getty ImagesAttorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel on Tuesday dodged questions about the conclusions of an investigation President Donald Trump cited to push Nvidia's board to bring back Jensen Huang as CEO.Asked by a reporter whether the Department of Justice had investigated Huang and the results of that probe, Blanche said, "What the president said is that he talked to a lot of people going into the decision that he made to encourage the board to reinstate him.""And so I'm not going to get into communications I have with the president," Blanche said at a news conference in Washington, D.C.Huang was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia on Monday morning, less than two weeks after resigning amid allegation had had affairs with a purported spy for China and two Nvidia employees, as well as concerns that advance semiconductor chips made by his company had been diverted to China in violation of U.S. law.In an interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump was asked what led him to personally confirm to Nvidia's board that Huang was not a national security risk."We've done a very thorough investigation, and the investigation showed that he did, I mean, he had bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents, but he did nothing wrong," Trump replied.Trump in a Truth Social post on Monday said the U.S. government had no reason to believe Huang's return to the company "poses any risk to National Security," and that Blanche had confirmed the government "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."Nvidia, in its statement Monday announcing Huang's return, said, "The Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk."Read more Nvidia newsNvidia shares fall as Huang comeback rally coolsAG Blanche, FBI's Patel dodge questions about Huang investigationCongress blasts Nvidia bringing Jensen Huang backJensen Huang to face Congress the same day as Nvidia GTCWhat Jensen Huang's return means for Nvidia's Colette KressTrump: 'I made the deal' to reinstate Nvidia's HuangNvidia surge: What investors should do with the stock and the AI trade nowBlanche on Tuesday said, "Nvidia is a good corporate citizen.""Obviously, if Nvidia was the target, or was the subject of some criminal investigation, or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people," Blanche said.Patel did not answer a reporter's question of whether the FBI has spoken to Huang, and whether the FBI had been made aware of an assessment by U.S. intelligence agencies that Huang's reported paramour, Alice Huang, was an asset for China's spy agency. Jensen Huang is not related to Alice Huang, who was an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia's semiconductor chips. The DOJ and Commerce Department on Nov. 17 said they were investigating Megaspeed for potential diversion of Nvidia chips in violation of U.S. export law. Asked how the DOJ could rule out Jensen Huang having potential criminal liability given the fact that the investigation remains ongoing, Blanche replied, "So, when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about.""We have hundreds, if not more, export investigations going at any time at the Department of Justice," Blanche said.

schema.headline: AG Blanche, FBI’s Patel dodge questions about Jensen Huang investigation

title: Best Buy reports comparable sales growth of 6.1%, highest in five years
description: A Grand Theft Auto VI advertisement is displayed at a Best Buy store at the Atlantic Terminal Mall on Nov. 19, 2026 in New York City. Michael M. Santi
body: A Grand Theft Auto VI advertisement is displayed at a Best Buy store at the Atlantic Terminal Mall on Nov. 19, 2026 in New York City. Michael M. Santiago | Getty ImagesBest Buy on Tuesday beat Wall Street expectations on the top and bottom lines for its third fiscal quarter and raised its full-year guidance.The consumer electronics retailer reported comparable sales growth of 6.1%, a significant beat over expectations of 2.3%, according to market intelligence platform StreetAccount. The company said that growth was its highest in five years. It reported a domestic comparable sales increase of 6.2% and international comparable sales growth of 4.9%."We have a tremendous amount of momentum," CEO Jason Bonfig told CNBC. "The fact that we saw pretty much broad-based growth across almost all of our categories is a lot of momentum that we're very excited about."Best Buy also raised its guidance for the rest of the year. It's now expecting full-year revenue of between $43 billion and $43.3 billion compared with a previous expectation of between $42.3 billion and $42.8 billion. It's expecting comparable sales to be up 3.4% to 4% compared with prior guidance of between 1.9% and 3%. The earnings report is the company's first since Bonfig took over as CEO from Corie Barry at the beginning of the month.Bonfig said the retailer saw overperformance in both computing and gaming for the quarter, driven by recent game launches and a targeted product assortment. Looking ahead into the holiday season, he said the Best Buy consumer remains "resilient," but that they are focused on getting value wherever they can."We did see not only our current customers continue to be engaged, but we actually did see more new customers come into the brand, as well as we had some customers that we re-engaged as well," Bonfig said. "So those are really, really positive signs for us in Q3, and all of that was factored into the way that we guided for Q4 and the rest of the year."Here's how the company performed in the period ended Oct. 31 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:Earnings per share: $1.62 adjusted vs. $1.49 expectedRevenue: $10.24 billion vs. $9.90 billion expectedBest Buy reported net income of $353 million, or $1.66 per share, compared with $140 million, or 66 cents per share, the year prior. Adjusting for one-time items, including restructuring charges, Best Buy posted adjusted earnings of $1.62 per share.Revenue rose to $10.24 billion from $9.67 billion in the year-ago period. Best Buy reported domestic revenue of $9.42 billion and international revenue of $820 million.Tuesday's earnings are the latest in a series of strong reports from the retailer, which has been instituting a turnaround strategy to return to growth after getting hit by declining foot traffic, lower consumer sentiment, tariffs and memory costs. Shares of Best Buy are up nearly 45% this year. Bonfig told CNBC last quarter that the launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI" in the current quarter is expected to drive sales in the gaming category, which has been seeing gains over the past year. Last month, Best Buy launched a new gaming experience for customers featuring gaming content, technology and special offers, among other features. "I think there'll still be opportunities for gaming to continue to drive our business moving forward," Bonfig told CNBC on Tuesday.

schema.headline: Best Buy reports comparable sales growth of 6.1%, highest in five years

title: Trump Account contributions from friends and family pass $1 billion mark, Treasury says
description: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent speaking on CNBC's Squawk Box on Nov. 13, 2026.CNBCFamilies and friends have collectively contributed more than $1 bi
body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent speaking on CNBC's Squawk Box on Nov. 13, 2026.CNBCFamilies and friends have collectively contributed more than $1 billion to Trump Accounts since the July 4 launch, bringing total deposits to more than $9 billion, the U.S. Department of the Treasury said Tuesday in an announcement exclusively provided to CNBC. The $1 billion in Trump Account deposits come from more than 3 million individuals, according to the agency. That total does not include the government's seed money or philanthropic gifts from donors such as Michael and Susan Dell. "The American people are investing in Trump Accounts with a generosity that represents the finest instincts of our national character," U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a written statement."Trump Accounts are a transformative government program for American children. It is the largest government start-up in American history," Internal Revenue Service CEO Frank Bisignano said in the statement.Also known as 530A accounts, Trump Accounts are open to any U.S. child under 18 with a Social Security number.Parents, guardians, grandparents and others can collectively contribute up to $5,000 per child per year in after-tax dollars up until the year before the beneficiary turns 18. The annual contribution limit is indexed for inflation after 2027. Children born from 2025 through 2028 may receive a one-time $1,000 deposit from the Treasury. Other funds may also be available, depending on certain criteria. Most recently, Snowflake chairman Frank Slootman and his wife, Brenda, announced they would give $1,000 to every child in Montana born in 2023 and 2024.The Treasury rolled out temporary regulations at the end of September that allow Trump Accounts to hold stock donations, a move meant to pave the way for more philanthropic gifts, according to Bisignano.These rules make it more attractive for donors, according to Ben Henry-Moreland, a certified financial planner with advisor platform Kitces.com. Wealthy founders and shareholders can avoid the capital gains taxes that would otherwise be triggered by selling appreciated stock and donating the cash proceeds. However, it also means some children's wealth accumulation could be tied to the performance of individual companies.Future Trump Account giftsThe Trump Accounts milestone comes as more billionaires and companies pledge support to the investment account for kids.In an exclusive interview with CNBC's "Squawk on the Street," Bessent on Nov. 20 announced an Anthropic co-founder would make a "large gift" to Trump Accounts over the next few weeks.A source briefed on the announcement confirmed that the Anthropic co-founder Bessent referred to is Tom Brown and that it is part of his broader philanthropic plan. "This is the perfect vehicle to donate to the children of America, and they will receive 100% of the proceeds," Bessent said.Elon Musk wrote in an X post that he plans to give every kid in America a share of SpaceX sometime in 2027, which experts say may come via Trump Accounts. watch nowIn a separate funding announcement, SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said she would donate around 2 million shares of her and her husband's SpaceX stock to the accounts.On Monday, Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, founder of Invest America and an architect of Trump Accounts, told CNBC's "Halftime Report" that more large-scale donations may be in the pipeline. "I want everybody to own shares of Nvidia, in Anthropic, in OpenAI," he said. "We created 70 million stock accounts — free stock accounts — for every single citizen under the age of 18 to do just that, and we have huge announcements coming."Subscribe to CNBC on YouTube.

schema.headline: Trump Account contributions from friends and family pass $1 billion mark, Treasury says

title: China has changed tactics but is still thwarting India's rise, a U.S. panel says
description: A conceptual image depicting the strained relationship between India and China, symbolized by their respective national flags painted on cracked and w
body: A conceptual image depicting the strained relationship between India and China, symbolized by their respective national flags painted on cracked and weathered surfaces, separated by a jagged, dividing line. Zpagistock | Moment | Getty ImagesChina is "actively working to suppress India's rise," even as the relationship between the two major Asian powers has thawed in the past year, according to a U.S. panel that sees an opening for greater outreach to India.On Nov. 18, a U.S. China Economic and Security Review Commission report said Beijing is applying military, economic, maritime, and other forms of pressure to constrain India.China has recalled engineers and withheld equipment to slow India's electronics manufacturing, slashed pharmaceutical input prices to undercut new Indian plants, and imposed export controls on battery technology to impede the development of India's clean energy industry, the report said.It added that these tensions offer the U.S. an opportunity to counter growing Chinese influence by building closer ties with India across key sectors such as pharmaceutical and defense. Ties have improved since a deadly border skirmish in 2020, but experts told CNBC that trust is still thin between Beijing and New Delhi. However, they added that the uneasy peace with China is unlikely to make India align automatically with the U.S. as an ally.The Indian foreign and commerce ministries and the Chinese foreign ministry did not respond to emails seeking comments.Chinese disruptionThe thawing in relations between India and China came amid industrial demand, as well as the need for "a whole lot of posturing for the U.S.," said Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at strategic advisory firm Teneo.Over the past year, India faced tariff pressures and needed to signal to Washington that its options remain open, including that of renegotiating relations with China, he explained, but added that as the trade deal with the U.S. is "close enough now," there is no pressing need for that signaling.Further improvement in the relationship is also limited by reports of renewed border tensions between the two sides and Beijing's scant reciprocation on easing access to technology and people movement, he said.Last month, an Indian military official said that confrontations with Chinese soldiers were ongoing across several locations along the country's northeastern border, even as top leaders from the countries met with fanfare at the BRICS Summit in September.Another flash point was when Beijing put export controls on tunnel boring machines last month. "Our relations with China remain good, and if there aren't any new hurdles, they can improve further," India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal reportedly said after China's move to tighten TBM exports. On Monday, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson reportedly said Beijing is ready to work with India to facilitate visa arrangements for business personnel from both sides amid reports that fewer Indian businessmen got visas to attend an annual trade fair in Shanghai.The Chinese "actively disrupt" areas where India is trying to make progress in terms of moving global supply chains, developing advanced industrial technologies such as EVs, batteries, electronic components, and pharmaceutical ingredients, Pramit Pal Chaudhuri, South Asia practice head at Eurasia Group, told CNBC.He added China is increasingly focused on containing India economically rather than through military overtures. India's manufacturing push still relies on Chinese inputs, from electronics components and solar materials to rare earth magnets and specialized machinery. Between April and October, India imported goods worth $96.6 billion from China, up more than 30% from a year ago, as per commerce ministry data released earlier this month.Its major imports from China include electronic goods, machinery, chemicals, transport equipment, iron and steel, and pharmaceutical products. While India needs inputs for its manufacturing ambitions from Beijing and China values access to Indian markets, trust between the two sides is "still thin," according to Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, citing a large trade imbalance and overlapping interests in South Asia and the Indian Ocean as additional issues.

schema.headline: China has changed tactics but is still thwarting India's rise, a U.S. panel says

title: Congress shreds Nvidia's 'outrageous' decision to bring back Huang: 'Failure of character'
description: Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., talks with reporters outside the Capitol Hill Club after a meeting of the House Republican Conference on June 24, 2026.Tom Wil
body: Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., talks with reporters outside the Capitol Hill Club after a meeting of the House Republican Conference on June 24, 2026.Tom Williams | Cq-roll Call, Inc. | Getty ImagesMembers of Congress from both parties on Monday expressed outrage and incredulity, and doubled down on their calls for investigations, after Nvidia announced it has reinstated Jensen Huang as its president and CEO.The resurrection of Huang, who had resigned from the artificial intelligence behemoth just 11 days earlier, raises more questions about the company's decision-making and the Trump administration's national security assessments, on top of existing concerns about Nvidia's advanced AI chips being diverted to China, the lawmakers said."It's inexplicable to me why they want this guy back as CEO," Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., a China hawk who is retiring from Congress, told CNBC in a phone interview. "To me it's a failure of character."President Donald Trump told CNBC in an extended interview later Monday morning that he personally intervened to convince Nvidia's board to bring Huang back, saying, "I made the deal."watch nowBacon, chairman of the House Subcommittee on Cyber, Information Technologies, and Innovation, said he wants the next Congress to conduct thorough oversight, while questioning the Trump administration's motives."Somebody's responsible for this, and it may be" Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department is responsible for setting U.S. export controls on AI chips, Bacon said. "But I think we should get to the bottom of this." Huang, who is scheduled to testify before multiple committees on Capitol Hill starting Dec. 1, is "going to get high scrutiny in a bipartisan way when he comes next week," Bacon said.Huang's closed-door appearance before a trio of House committees is on the schedule, as the panels seek answers on the national security implications of Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, MS NOW reported. The Senate banking committee announced after Huang's reinstatement that he will appear for a public hearing Dec. 3.John Fisher of Trident, a spokesman for Huang, declined to comment on the Nvidia CEO's scheduled appearances.Read more Nvidia newsNvidia shares fall as Huang comeback rally coolsAG Blanche, FBI's Patel dodge questions about Huang investigationCongress blasts Nvidia bringing Jensen Huang backJensen Huang to face Congress the same day as Nvidia GTCWhat Jensen Huang's return means for Nvidia's Colette KressTrump: 'I made the deal' to reinstate Nvidia's HuangNvidia surge: What investors should do with the stock and the AI trade now"He better be there," Rep. Gabe Amo, D-R.I., a member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told CNBC about Huang's scheduled Dec. 1 appearance. His reinstatement will only intensify congressional probes into Nvidia and its government connections, Amo predicted."I think it frankly broadens the scope of the query, and it makes Howard Lutnick and his dealings — supporting his nepo children's operation at Cantor Fitzgerald — party to inquiry as well as any other administration official that has facilitated a status quo in which chips can be sold to China or Chinese operated intermediaries who don't intend good things for the American people," said Amo, referring to the financial firm run by Lutnick's sons that has business ties to Nvidia.A Cantor spokesperson didn't comment directly when asked about Amo's comments, saying the firm "holds no material proprietary position in Nvidia" and noting its Nvidia positions "arise primarily from equity swaps executed for clients."The Commerce Department didn't immediately respond to requests to comment on Bacon's and Amo's remarks.Nvidia in a statement Monday said it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and that it is confident that Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk."Stock Chart IconStock chart iconNvidia StockDavid Rudenstine, a constitutional law professor and national security scholar at Cardozo School of Law, said the frenzy around Huang's comeback is secondary to lingering national security concerns."The real responsibility for national security is with the administration and not with the CEO of a private company," Rudenstine told CNBC."You're opposed to China getting the chips. You recognize that the intermediary companies are sending chips to China, and you don't put a stop to it. I don't get it," he said.Capitol Hill doubles down on criticismThe CEO's reinstatement, while celebrated by the White House and in Silicon Valley, led to heightened calls on Capitol Hill to seek answers on AI chip exports to China and what the Trump administration's role has been in facilitating that."We are sending high-end computer chips to China, and yet we're saying we want to win the AI war. It's a contradiction, and it's a failure of leadership in the White House," Bacon told CNBC.Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, told CNBC in an emailed statement that Huang's return "proves that under Trump, Vance, and Rubio, national security is for sale to the highest bidder.""We will all pay the price of letting China plunder America's cutting edge technology. Democrats will be pushing for accountability for anyone in the administration that put corrupt deals over our country's security," Wyden, who is also a Senate Intelligence Committee member, said.Trump in a Truth Social post Monday added that Attorney General Todd Blanche "has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."Lawmakers, who have already launched multiple investigations related to Huang, Nvidia and related entities, quickly filed in to question those conclusions. Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., a close Trump ally and a former CEO,  criticized the move and called for a congressional briefing "as soon as possible" on Huang's reinstatement."Nvidia's board is free to vote however they want, but the federal government owes the American people answers about what actually happened," Scott told CNBC in an emailed statement. "This looks terrible on its face, and it drives home the need for Congress to be informed on the full impact of Jensen Huang's actions on our national security and economy."Rep. Scott Peters, D-Calif., a member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, told CNBC that it's still not clear to what degree Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy might have compromised national security."The fact that the president of the United States is involved in putting him back in there, presumably because maybe he has stock or he just cares about the stock market, it's really reached a bizarre place," Peters said. "And obviously that man has not learned anything from the election about what people think of him, or he doesn't care."Monday's move also gave fuel to lawmakers who have already questioned Trump, his administration or Nvidia."The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said in a statement via the Senate Banking Committee, where she is the top Democrat and is expected to become chair in January.Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, more tersely questioned the official assurances that Huang poses no risks to national security. "No national security risk? Based on what?" he wrote on X.Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill., who serves on the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, in an X post called Nvidia's decision to reinstate Huang "outrageous.""We still don't know what information Chinese intelligence may have obtained from him, and neither the government nor Nvidia's own board has completed its investigation," wrote Krishnamoorthi, who is also a member of the House Oversight and Intelligence panels.— CNBC's Dan Mangan, Garrett Downs and Luke Fountain contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Congress shreds Nvidia's 'outrageous' decision to bring back Huang: 'Failure of character'

title: Jensen Huang is ‘too big to fire,’ putting Nvidia’s governance in focus: analysts
description: Co-founder, President and CEO of US Technology company Nvidia, Jensen Huang, looks on during a press briefing in Paris on October 13, 2026. (Photo by
body: Co-founder, President and CEO of US Technology company Nvidia, Jensen Huang, looks on during a press briefing in Paris on October 13, 2026. (Photo by JOEL SAGET / AFP via Getty Images)Joel Saget | Afp | Getty ImagesJensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO may have eased concerns over the chipmaker's leadership, but it has also brought renewed scrutiny to the company's corporate governance and its reliance on its founder.Huang's abrupt departure and unexpected reinstatement exposed a deeper vulnerability at the heart of Nvidia, industry experts told CNBC, raising questions about board oversight and succession planning. "What does it mean if you have a company too big to fail or a CEO too big to fire?" Angela Mancini, head of advisory for global risk insights at Dow Jones, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Tuesday. Mancini pointed to Huang's unusually large number of direct reports as another sign of how heavily Nvidia depends on its founder."What does it mean when someone has 60 direct reports, and you literally are in a situation where you feel like you can't fire them?" she added.Nvidia's market cap ballooned from $3 trillion on Friday to almost $4 trillion on Tuesday after Huang was reinstated. "That is what you'd call a founder premium," Yang Wang, a principal analyst at Counterpoint Research, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe." "The reaction has been staggering," Wang said. "But is this level of dependence healthy?"For Nvidia, Huang's return offers an opportunity to address some of the governance issues brought to light by his departure.An opportunity for changeJeff Herbst, managing partner at GFT Ventures and a former Nvidia executive who spent nearly two decades at the company, said he had written to the board late last week calling for Huang's return.While initially disappointed by the allegations surrounding Huang, Herbst said he came to view the episode as an opportunity for Nvidia to strengthen its governance, succession planning and overall management.watch now"While a lot of people saw a crisis here, I saw a potential opportunity," he said.Herbst said Nvidia's management and oversight functions needed to evolve alongside its transformation from a relatively small technology company into one of the world's largest corporations."I think the corporate governance, the succession planning, the legal function, the regulatory function, the political function, all has to scale at the same time," he said.He suggested Nvidia add more experience to its board by bringing in individuals who have run large companies and take a more formal approach to developing potential successors to Huang.watch nowTom Hulick, CEO of Strategy Asset Managers, agreed, saying the chip giant's "corporate governance definitely needs to be retooled." It's "unheard of" and "unprecedented" for a president to enforce the reinstatement of a company's CEO, Hulick said on "Squawk Box Europe" on Tuesday."He's a born leader. He's enduring a lot of pain right now. Does he deserve to be back as CEO? It's not for me to speculate. Is he the right person? Probably for now." However, Hulick added that the company still has "a lot of things to worry about" regarding corporate governance. The succession questionHuang's departure also exposed how closely Nvidia's leadership and long-term strategy are tied to its founder, raising questions about how the company would navigate a future transition.Stacy Rasgon, managing director and senior U.S. semiconductor analyst at Bernstein Research, said the episode had revived attention to a risk investors had long overlooked.watch now"We all knew that there was key man risk here. We all chose, and I'm including myself in that. We all kind of chose to just ignore it," Rasgon told CNBC.Succession planning, he said, is an issue both Huang and the board will need to address and communicate clearly to investors."I think both Jensen and the board will have to figure out, and I think communicate to investors," he added. Herbst also pointed to Huang's personal role in driving Nvidia's technological innovations, including his willingness to invest in artificial intelligence and high-performance computing long before those businesses became profitable.New markets such as autonomous systems and robotics would require major investment and a leader with Huang's passion and vision, Herbst added. Correction: This story has been updated to reflect that Angela Mancini said Nvidia is in a situation where it feels like you can not fire the CEO.

schema.headline: Jensen Huang is ‘too big to fire,’ putting Nvidia’s governance in focus: analysts
